claim: Sepsis causes millions of deaths per year worldwide and is a current global health priority declared by the WHO.
source: Sepsis causes millions of deaths per year worldwide and is a current global health priority declared by the WHO.
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO declaration and global health statistics

claim: Extracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is released by inflamed host cells and tissues.
source: An important mediator of inflammation is extracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) that is released by inflamed host cells and tissues
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about ATP release

claim: Bacteria release ATP in a strain-specific and growth-dependent manner.
source: An important mediator of inflammation is extracellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) that is released by inflamed host cells and tissues, and also by bacteria in a strain-specific and growth-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: ATP release by E. coli is dependent on ATP synthase within the inner bacterial membrane.
source: Using genetic mutant strains of Escherichia coli (E. coli), we demonstrate that ATP release is dependent on ATP synthase within the inner bacterial membrane.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using genetic mutants

claim: Impaired integrity of the outer bacterial membrane contributes to ATP release and is associated with bacterial death.
source: In addition, impaired integrity of the outer bacterial membrane notably contributes to ATP release and is associated with bacterial death.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from porin mutants

claim: Bacterial ATP suppresses local immune responses, resulting in reduced neutrophil counts and impaired survival.
source: Abrogating bacterial ATP release shows that bacterial ATP suppresses local immune responses, resulting in reduced neutrophil counts and impaired survival.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from apyrase-expressing bacteria in mouse model

claim: Bacterial ATP has systemic effects via its transport in outer membrane vesicles (OMV).
source: In addition, bacterial ATP has systemic effects via its transport in outer membrane vesicles (OMV).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ATP in OMV

claim: ATP-loaded OMV are quickly distributed throughout the body.
source: ATP-loaded OMV are quickly distributed throughout the body and upregulated expression of genes activating degranulation in neutrophils, potentially contributing to the exacerbation of sepsis severity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from OMV injection experiments

claim: ATP-loaded OMV upregulate expression of genes activating degranulation in neutrophils.
source: ATP-loaded OMV are quickly distributed throughout the body and upregulated expression of genes activating degranulation in neutrophils, potentially contributing to the exacerbation of sepsis severity.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data from pulmonary neutrophils

claim: 11 million sepsis-related deaths were reported in 2017, accounting for 19.7% of all global deaths.
source: Worldwide, 11 million sepsis-related deaths were reported in 2017, which accounted for an estimated 19.7% of all global deaths (Rudd et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rudd et al., 2020

claim: The World Health Organization has declared sepsis as a global health priority.
source: Given its high incidence and immense socio-economic burden, the World Health Organization (WHO) has declared sepsis as a global health priority (Reinhart et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinhart et al., 2017

claim: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by an imbalanced host immune response to infection.
source: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by an imbalanced host immune response to infection.
evidence: Supported by established medical definition

claim: Despite the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, lethality from sepsis remains high.
source: Antibiotic treatment remains the main approach to treat sepsis; however, despite the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, lethality remains high.
evidence: Supported by clinical knowledge and literature

claim: Most trials inhibiting cytokine responses or Toll-like receptors have failed.
source: Until recently however, most trials inhibiting cytokine responses or Toll-like receptors failed, indicating that alternative approaches for immunomodulation are required (Cao et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cao et al., 2023

claim: Extracellular ATP critically modulates inflammatory and immune responses by activating ionotropic P2X and metabotropic P2Y receptors.
source: It has been shown that adenosine triphosphate (ATP), as soon as it is released into the extracellular space, critically modulates inflammatory and immune responses (Di Virgilio et al., 2020; Eltzschig et al., 2012) by activating ionotropic P2X and metabotropic P2Y receptors (Burnstock, 2020; Junger, 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Purinergic signaling critically alters immune responses during sepsis.
source: Also, such purinergic signaling critically alters immune responses during sepsis (Dosch et al., 2019; Ledderose et al., 2016; Spari and Beldi, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Connexin-dependent release of ATP by macrophages initiates an autocrine loop of over-activation, resulting in altered local and systemic cytokine secretion that exacerbates abdominal sepsis.
source: In particular, we have described that the connexin-dependent release of ATP by macrophages initiates an autocrine loop of over-activation, resulting in altered local and systemic cytokine secretion, which exacerbates abdominal sepsis (Dosch et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dosch et al., 2019

claim: Bacteria release ATP into the extracellular space.
source: Recently, it has been discovered that also bacteria release ATP into the extracellular space (Mempin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mempin et al., 2013

claim: ATP release has been shown for E. coli, K. pneumoniae, E. faecalis, and S. aureus.
source: ATP release has been shown for a variety of bacteria including the sepsis-associated Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (K. pneumoniae) from the Proteobacteria phylum or Enterococcus faecalis (E. faecalis) and Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) from the Firmicutes phylum (Diekema et al., 2019; Hironaka et al., 2013; Iwase et al., 2010; Mempin et al., 2013; Mureșan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: ATP released by mutualistic bacteria in the intestine modulates local cellular and secretory immune responses.
source: In colonized compartments such as the intestine, it has been shown that ATP released by mutualistic bacteria modulates local cellular and secretory immune responses (Atarashi et al., 2008; Perruzza et al., 2017; Proietti et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Bacterial ATP release in the mouth leads to biofilm dispersal and periodontitis.
source: and in the mouth, bacterial ATP release leads to biofilm dispersal and periodontitis (Ding et al., 2016a; Ding and Tan, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ding et al., 2016a and Ding and Tan, 2016b

claim: Twenty-five different colonies were randomly picked from abdominal fluid of patients with abdominal sepsis and analyzed by whole 16S-rRNA Sanger sequencing, resulting in 12 different bacterial species.
source: Twenty-five different colonies were randomly picked and analyzed by whole 16S-rRNA Sanger sequencing, which resulted in 12 different bacterial species (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 1B

claim: A growth-dependent release of ATP was observed in all assessed sepsis-associated bacterial species, peaking during exponential growth phase.
source: A growth-dependent release of ATP was observed in all species, peaking during exponential growth phase (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: ATP release was detected across all assessed bacterial species from patients.
source: ATP release was detected across all assessed species (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: In the mouse model, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes phyla were predominating, similar to human samples.
source: Similar to human samples, Proteobacteria and Firmicutes phyla were predominating (Figure 1F, see Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1F and 1B

claim: In the mouse model, E. coli released notably more cumulative ATP compared to E. faecalis and S. aureus.
source: In the mouse model, E. coli released notably more cumulative ATP compared to E. faecalis and S. aureus (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G and 1H

claim: The bacterial species assessed in humans and mice differed on the strain level, confirming that ATP release is strain-specific.
source: The bacterial species assessed in humans and mice (E. coli, E. faecalis, S. aureus) differed on the strain level (sequences deposited, see Data availability statement) confirming that ATP release is strain-specific (Mempin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Mempin et al., 2013

claim: Mutations in subunits of ATP synthase were generally associated with significantly lower cumulative ATP release compared to mutations in cytochrome bo3 oxidase subunits.
source: We first noticed that mutations in subunits of ATP synthase, which is the key enzyme of ATP generation, were generally associated with significantly lower cumulative ATP release compared to mutations in cytochrome bo3 oxidase subunits (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Cumulative ATP release and cumulative growth were positively correlated.
source: We determined cumulative growth (AUC growth) in addition to cumulative ATP release and indeed, cumulative ATP release and cumulative growth were positively correlated (Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Peak ATP and peak growth (OD600) are positively correlated.
source: similar to peak ATP and peak growth (OD600) that are positively correlated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Cumulative ATP release from the porin mutants were notably different compared to the parental strain, being lowest in ΔompC and highest in ΔompF.
source: Cumulative ATP release (AUC ATP) from the porin mutants were notably different compared to the PS, being lowest in ΔompC and highest in ΔompF (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3B and 3C

claim: There was a strong negative correlation between the individual peak of released ATP and growth at the same time point.
source: There was a strong negative correlation between the individual peak of released ATP (marked by the red line in Figure 3B) and growth at the same time point (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figures 3B and 3D

claim: Outer membrane integrity and bacterial death are significantly increased in ΔompF compared to ΔompC and the parental strain after 4 hr of culturing.
source: Indeed, outer membrane integrity and bacterial death are significantly increased in ΔompF compared to ΔompC and the PS after 4 hr (ATP peak) of culturing (Figure 3E and F)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3E and 3F

claim: Destabilization of the outer bacterial membrane results in bacterial death that is associated with ATP release.
source: We conclude from these data that destabilization of the outer bacterial membrane (as observed with the ΔompF mutant) results in bacterial death that is associated with ATP release.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on porin mutants

claim: Apyrase induction resulted in a significant reduction of ATP release in PS+pAPY compared to PS+pEMPTY.
source: Indeed, apyrase induction resulted in a significant reduction of ATP release in PS+pAPY, compared to PS+pEMPTY (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: ATP release was abrogated in the bacteria cultures that were used for injection.
source: Thereby ATP release was abrogated in the bacteria cultures that were used for injection (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: No difference in ATP levels was detected in abdominal fluid after 4 and 8 hr following bacterial injection.
source: In vivo, no difference in ATP levels was detected when ATP was measured directly in the abdominal fluid after 4 (Figure 4C) and 8 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: No differences in local or systemic bacterial counts were observed after 4 and 8 hr following bacterial injection.
source: After both 4 (Figure 4D and E) and 8 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E), no differences in local or systemic bacterial counts were observed.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: Survival was significantly higher in the absence of bacterial ATP (PS+pAPY) compared to ATP-generating controls (PS+pEMPTY) after intraabdominal injection.
source: Yet, despite similar bacterial counts, the survival was significantly higher in the absence of bacterial ATP (PS+pAPY) compared to ATP-generating controls (PS+pEMPTY) after i.a. injection (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 4F

claim: A disappearance reaction of large peritoneal macrophages (LPM) was observed after E. coli injection compared to sham controls after 4 and 8 hr.
source: As expected, a disappearance reaction of large peritoneal macrophages (LPM) was observed after both, E. coli PS+pEMPTY and E. coli PS+pAPY, i.a. injection compared to sham controls after 4 (Figure 4H) and 8 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F; Ghosn et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, and citation to Ghosn et al., 2010

claim: The number of small peritoneal macrophages (SPM) and CX3CR1pos monocytes was significantly reduced, whereas neutrophils were significantly increased in bacterial ATP-depleted abdominal sepsis.
source: Interestingly, however, the number of small peritoneal macrophages (SPM) and CX3CR1pos monocytes was significantly reduced, whereas neutrophils were significantly increased almost up to 8 hr (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) in bacterial ATP-depleted abdominal sepsis (PS+pAPY).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G

claim: The ΔnlpI and ΔtolB strains showed a 20- and 30-fold increase of OMV when compared with the parental strain.
source: The ΔnlpI and ΔtolB strains showed a 20- and 30-fold increase of OMV when compared with the PS (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: ATP was detected in OMV from all assessed strains at the individual peak of ATP release but only in minimal detectable levels after 24 hr.
source: ATP was detected in OMV from all assessed strains at the individual peak of ATP release but only in minimal detectable levels after 24 hr (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: ΔtolB OMV were equipped with outer membrane ompF but not cytoplasmic ftsZ, indicating that they are outer membrane derived.
source: They were equipped with outer membrane ompF but not cytoplasmic ftsZ (Figure 5D), indicating that they are outer membrane derived.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D

claim: OMV were loaded with ATP using electroporation.
source: OMV were loaded with ATP (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Over time, the amount of ATP in OMV decreased, especially at physiological (37°C) temperature.
source: and over time, the amount of ATP in OMV decreased, especially at physiological (37°C) temperature (Figure 5G) as opposed to 4°C (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Uptake of DiI-stained OMV by leukocytes in the abdominal fluid was independent of ATP cargo.
source: In the abdominal fluid, uptake of DiI-stained OMV by leukocytes was independent of ATP cargo (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: All major cell populations with phagocytic ability (LPM, SPM, neutrophils) were highly positive for OMV.
source: and all major cell populations with phagocytic ability (LPM, SPM, neutrophils) were highly positive for OMV (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B

claim: LPM dramatically decreased, whereas neutrophils increased in response to OMV when compared to sham controls.
source: LPM dramatically decreased, whereas neutrophils increased in response to OMV when compared to sham controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C

claim: Within 1 hr, DiI-stained OMV were distributed throughout the body and mainly taken up by neutrophils.
source: Within 1 hr, the DiI-stained OMV were distributed throughout the body and mainly taken up by neutrophils, with remarkable differences between organs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B, C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B, and C

claim: The highest ratio of OMVpos neutrophils compared to all other OMVpos cells was observed in the lung in an ATP-independent manner.
source: The highest ratio of OMVpos neutrophils compared to all other OMVpos cells was observed in the lung in an ATP-independent manner (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C

claim: A strong co-localization of OMV with the endolysosomal compartment of pulmonary neutrophils was identified.
source: A strong co-localization with the endolysosomal compartment of pulmonary neutrophils was identified (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Uptake of ATP-loaded OMV resulted in a significantly different transcriptional activity compared to empty OMV in pulmonary neutrophils.
source: Uptake of ATP-loaded OMV resulted in a significantly different transcriptional activity compared to empty OMV (Figure 6E)
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The strongest differences in transcriptional activity were found in lysosomal and neutrophil degranulation pathways.
source: The strongest differences were found in lysosomal and neutrophil degranulation pathways (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 5

claim: In the lysosomal pathway, transcripts for proteins involved in autophagosome-lysosome fusion, endosome to lysosome transport, or enzymatic cleavage were significantly higher expressed in response to ATP-loaded OMV.
source: In the lysosomal pathway, transcripts for proteins involved in autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Gabarap), endosome to lysosome transport (Hgsnat, Laptm5), or enzymatic cleavage (Capn1, Fuca1, Ctsb, Ctsd, Gba) were significantly higher expressed in response to ATP-loaded OMV when compared to empty OMV (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figures 6F and 6G

claim: Neutrophil degranulation was significantly increased in response to ATP-loaded OMV as indicated by increased expression of gene transcripts resulting in antibacterial activity and NETosis.
source: Furthermore, neutrophil degranulation was significantly increased in response to ATP-loaded OMV as indicated by increased expression of gene transcripts resulting in antibacterial activity (Lyz2, S100a8, Camp) or NETosis (Tlr2, Itgb2) (Figure 6F and H).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figures 6F and 6H

claim: ATP synthase is most likely dominant compared to cytochrome bo3 oxidase because of its non-redundant function for ATP generation and bacterial growth.
source: ATP synthase is most likely dominant compared to cytochrome bo3 oxidase because of its non-redundant function for ATP generation and bacterial growth.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on mutants

claim: Mutations in one of the cytochrome bo3 oxidase subunits cyoA, cyoC, or cyoD could be compensated by another subunit.
source: Mutations in one of the cytochrome bo3 oxidase subunits cyoA, cyoC, or cyoD could be compensated by another subunit.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing lower impact of these mutations

claim: Lower ATP release in the cyoB mutant is supported by the fact that cyoB harbors all three prosthetic groups of the cytochrome bo3 oxidase and is therefore indispensable for proper function.
source: This is supported by lower ATP release in the cyoB mutant, which harbors all three prosthetic groups of the cytochrome bo3 oxidase and is therefore indispensable for proper function (Tsubaki et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Tsubaki et al., 2000

claim: Deficiency in the bo3-type oxidase could be partially compensated by bd-type oxidases.
source: Alternatively, deficiency in the bo3-type oxidase could be partially compensated by bd-type oxidases (Borisov et al., 2011; Grauel et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Borisov et al., 2011 and Grauel et al., 2021

claim: Previous studies using Sytox/PI staining and microscopy did not identify bacterial death as a relevant source of extracellular ATP during exponential growth.
source: Previous studies used Sytox/PI staining and microscopy to identify bacterial death and did not identify bacterial death as a relevant source of extracellular ATP during exponential growth (Hironaka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hironaka et al., 2013

claim: Flow cytometry is a quantitatively more sensitive method than microscopy for detecting bacterial death.
source: Conversely, we used flow cytometry, a quantitatively more sensitive method, and our data demonstrated that impaired membrane integrity and bacterial death are critical for ATP release during growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using flow cytometry

claim: The gradient between intra- and extracellular ATP is approximately 100-1000× higher intracellularly.
source: Despite low rates of bacterial death during exponential growth (Koch, 1959), and a low ratio of dead to live bacteria, the high gradient between intra- and extracellular ATP (approximately 100–1000× higher) might be sufficient to explain the amount of released ATP measured (Leduc and van Heijenoort, 1980; Mempin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Koch, 1959; Leduc and van Heijenoort, 1980; and Mempin et al., 2013

claim: The concentration of ATP within OMV is sufficient to activate P2-type receptors in lysosomes.
source: ATP was detected within OMV and the concentration of ATP within OMV is sufficient to activate P2-type receptors in lysosomes (Araujo et al., 2020; Junger, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Araujo et al., 2020 and Junger, 2011

claim: OMV are released in response to environmental stresses like infection and sepsis.
source: Furthermore, OMV are released in response to environmental stresses like infection and sepsis (Kulp and Kuehn, 2010; Orench-Rivera and Kuehn, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kulp and Kuehn, 2010 and Orench-Rivera and Kuehn, 2016

claim: P2X1, P2X3, and P2X4 receptors have been shown to be expressed in lysosomes.
source: ATP is likely to activate P2 receptors, which have been shown to be expressed in lysosomes, such as P2X1, P2X3, or P2X4 (Qureshi et al., 2007; Robinson and Murrell-Lagnado, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Qureshi et al., 2007 and Robinson and Murrell-Lagnado, 2013

claim: OMV can be considered as non-living bacteria-resembling highly inflammatory vesicles that effectively distribute ATP throughout the body.
source: OMV can therefore be considered as non-living bacteria-resembling highly inflammatory vesicles (Jang et al., 2015; Kulp and Kuehn, 2010) that effectively distribute ATP throughout the body to activate cells, such as neutrophils, initiating systemic inflammatory responses.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to Jang et al., 2015 and Kulp and Kuehn, 2010

claim: Activation of neutrophils in response to ATP-loaded OMV resulted in upregulation of inflammatory, lysosomal, and neutrophil degranulation pathways as well as an upregulation of the apoptosis pathway and genes involved in NETosis.
source: Activation of neutrophils in response to ATP-loaded OMV resulted in upregulation of inflammatory, lysosomal, and neutrophil degranulation pathways as well as an upregulation of the apoptosis pathway and genes involved in NETosis by a hitherto unknown mechanism.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data

claim: Remote degranulation in response to OMV is unlikely to control bacteria at the source of sepsis but rather harmful to host tissues increasing sepsis severity.
source: Such remote degranulation in response to OMV is unlikely to control bacteria at the source of sepsis but rather harmful to host tissues increasing sepsis severity (Eichelberger and Goldman, 2020).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citation to Eichelberger and Goldman, 2020

claim: Bacterial ATP release is strain specific.
source: Bacterial ATP release is strain specific (Figure 1; Mempin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and citation to Mempin et al., 2013

claim: The ΔtolB mutant produces only very few O-IMV (0.1-2% of all OMV).
source: However, the ΔtolB mutant produces, unlike other tol mutants, only very few O-IMV (0.1–2% of all OMV) (Pérez-Cruz et al., 2013; Reimer et al., 2021; Takaki et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pérez-Cruz et al., 2013; Reimer et al., 2021; and Takaki et al., 2020

claim: Western blot analysis suggests that the OMV used in this study are primarily outer membrane derived.
source: and our western blot analysis suggests that our OMV are primarily outer membrane derived.
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing presence of ompF and absence of ftsZ

claim: OMV are promising diagnostic molecular biomarkers in gram-negative sepsis.
source: OMV are promising diagnostic molecular biomarkers in gramneg sepsis (Michel and Gaborski, 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Michel and Gaborski, 2022

claim: ATP is involved in cell death and chemotaxis.
source: Since ATP is involved in cell death (Proietti et al., 2019) as well as in chemotaxis (Junger, 2011), increased cell death, impaired infiltration, or a combination of both is possible.
evidence: Supported by citations to Proietti et al., 2019 and Junger, 2011

claim: The human experimental protocol was approved by the Cantonal Ethics Commission Bern, Switzerland (ethical approval 2017-00573, NCT03554148).
source: The human experimental protocol was approved by the Cantonal Ethics Commission Bern, Switzerland (ethical approval 2017-00573, NCT03554148).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from all patients.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from all patients and the study has been performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki as well as the CONSORT statement.
evidence: Statement of ethical compliance

claim: All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Care Committee of the Canton of Bern (Switzerland) under the number BE41/2022.
source: All animal procedures were carried out in accordance with the Swiss guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals as well as in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines and were approved by the Animal Care Committee of the Canton of Bern (Switzerland) under the following number: BE41/2022.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval
